note: depth is derived: 1 + max(depth of prereqs). Roots are depth 0.

nodes.label: Fraction arithmetic
nodes.blurb: Can add, multiply, and divide fractions fluently, and knows why a common denominator is required.
misconceptions: adds numerators and denominators separately, so a/b + c/d becomes (a+c)/(b+d)
cancels a term across a sum, turning (x+2)/2 into x
inverts the wrong operand when dividing one fraction by another

nodes.label: Signed arithmetic
nodes.blurb: Handles negative quantities and sign distribution without dropping or misplacing minus signs.
misconceptions: reads the symbol -x as necessarily naming a negative number
distributes a leading minus over only the first term, so -(a+b) becomes -a+b
assumes subtracting a negative must make a result smaller

nodes.label: The coordinate plane
nodes.blurb: Treats a point as an ordered pair of numbers read against chosen axes, not as a mark on paper.
misconceptions: reverses the order of the pair, plotting (x, y) at (y, x)
thinks of a point as a dot on the page rather than a numeric readout that depends on the axes
cannot locate a point without gridlines to count along

nodes.label: Variables and expressions
nodes.blurb: Treats a letter as a number that varies and an expression as an object that can be rearranged.
misconceptions: reads a variable as a label for a thing ('c is cookies') rather than as a quantity
assumes different letters must stand for different values
treats an expression as an instruction to compute rather than an object to manipulate

nodes.label: Vector arithmetic
nodes.blurb: Adds and scales vectors componentwise and can picture the result as displacement in space.
misconceptions: believes a vector is pinned to the origin and cannot be translated
conflates a vector with its magnitude, treating it as a single number
adds vectors by joining lists rather than by matching components

nodes.label: Function notation
nodes.blurb: Reads f(x) as a machine applied to an input, independent of whether a formula is available.
misconceptions: reads f(x) as f multiplied by x
thinks f(x + 2) means f(x) + 2
believes a function must have a closed-form formula to be a function

nodes.label: Solving linear equations
nodes.blurb: Isolates an unknown by applying reversible operations to both sides while preserving balance.
misconceptions: moves a term across the equals sign without changing its sign
applies an operation to one side of the equation only
reads '=' as 'and then the answer is' rather than as an assertion that two things are equal

nodes.label: Linear combination
nodes.blurb: Sees scaling several vectors and adding them as a single reachable destination in space.
misconceptions: assumes the scalars must be positive, or must be whole numbers
believes a combination has to use every vector in the list
can compute one but cannot picture sweeping the scalars to reach a whole line or plane

nodes.label: Dot product
nodes.blurb: Computes it and reads it as a measure of how much one vector points along another.
misconceptions: expects the result to be a vector rather than a number
memorises the componentwise formula with no link to angle or projection
thinks a dot product of zero means one of the vectors must be the zero vector

nodes.label: Function composition
nodes.blurb: Applies f(g(x)) inside-out and understands the result as a single new function.
misconceptions: reads f(g(x)) left to right and applies f first
confuses composing functions with multiplying their outputs
assumes composition commutes, so f(g(x)) equals g(f(x))

nodes.label: Slope and lines
nodes.blurb: Connects the equation of a line to its geometry, and reads slope as a rate independent of drawing scale.
misconceptions: takes the coordinate differences in opposite orders in the numerator and denominator
judges slope by how steep the drawn picture looks, ignoring the axis scale
assumes any equation graphing as a straight line is a linear function

nodes.label: Span
nodes.blurb: Names the full set of points reachable by linear combinations, and pictures it as a line, plane, or space.
misconceptions: thinks span is the set of the given vectors themselves, not everything reachable from them
assumes n vectors always span n dimensions
pictures span as a finite collection of arrows rather than a continuous region

nodes.label: Matrix-vector product
nodes.blurb: Computes Av and reads the result as a linear combination of the columns of A.
misconceptions: multiplies elementwise, pairing entry against entry
executes the row-dot-vector algorithm but cannot see the output as a combination of A's columns
gets the shape rule backwards and pairs incompatible dimensions

nodes.label: Orthogonality
nodes.blurb: Uses a zero dot product as the definition of perpendicular, in any number of dimensions.
misconceptions: thinks orthogonality is a 2D picture with no meaning in higher dimensions
conflates orthogonal with linearly independent
believes the zero vector cannot be orthogonal to anything

nodes.label: Systems of equations
nodes.blurb: Solves several equations at once and reads the solution set as an intersection.
misconceptions: expects every system to have exactly one solution
reads 'no solution' as 'the solution is zero'
solves algebraically without connecting the answer to intersecting lines or planes

nodes.label: What 'linear' actually means
nodes.blurb: Tests a map for additivity and scaling rather than for the shape of its graph.
misconceptions: thinks 'linear' means 'graphs as a straight line', so f(x) = 2x + 3 counts
thinks any formula without exponents is linear
checks additivity but never scaling, or checks scaling but never additivity

nodes.label: Linear independence
nodes.blurb: Determines whether any vector in a set is redundant, i.e. already reachable from the others.
misconceptions: checks only pairs for being parallel, missing three-vector dependence
conflates independent with orthogonal
thinks a set containing the zero vector can still be independent

nodes.label: Projection
nodes.blurb: Finds the closest point in a subspace and recognises the leftover as orthogonal to it.
misconceptions: thinks projecting means deleting a coordinate
omits the normalisation, so the answer scales with the length of the target vector
does not see the residual as orthogonal to the thing projected onto

nodes.label: Gaussian elimination
nodes.blurb: Reduces a system with reversible row operations and reads the solution structure off the result.
misconceptions: uses operations that are not reversible, such as scaling a row by zero
operates on columns as though they were rows
reaches echelon form but cannot tell unique, absent, and infinite solution sets apart

nodes.label: Linear transformations
nodes.blurb: Sees a linear map as something acting on all of space at once, keeping grid lines parallel and the origin fixed.
misconceptions: thinks any function taking vectors to vectors is a linear transformation
believes a linear transformation can move the origin
pictures the map acting on one vector at a time rather than on the whole space

nodes.label: Basis
nodes.blurb: Recognises a minimal spanning set, and that a space admits many different bases.
misconceptions: thinks a space has one basis, the standard one
believes a basis must be orthogonal, or must consist of unit vectors
assumes adding more vectors gives a better basis

nodes.label: A matrix as a transformation
nodes.blurb: Reads the columns of a matrix as the landing spots of the basis vectors.
misconceptions: sees a matrix as a static grid of numbers rather than an encoding of where space goes
does not know the columns are the images of the basis vectors
thinks the matrix acts only on vectors written next to it, not on all of space

nodes.label: Null space
nodes.blurb: Identifies everything a transformation crushes to zero and links it to loss of dimension.
misconceptions: calls the null space empty when the only solution is the zero vector
confuses the null space with the zero matrix
cannot connect a nontrivial null space to the transformation collapsing space

nodes.label: Coordinates relative to a basis
nodes.blurb: Reads a coordinate list as a description relative to a chosen basis, not as the vector itself.
misconceptions: thinks a vector's coordinates are intrinsic to it rather than relative to a chosen basis
reads entries given in a new basis as if they were still standard-basis components
believes only the standard basis produces valid coordinates

nodes.label: Matrix multiplication
nodes.blurb: Computes a product and reads it as the composition of two transformations, applied right to left.
misconceptions: believes it is elementwise, like addition
executes the row-times-column algorithm but cannot say what the product represents
assumes AB equals BA because multiplication of numbers commutes

nodes.label: Determinant of a 2x2
nodes.blurb: Computes ad - bc and reads it as the factor by which area is scaled, sign included.
misconceptions: recalls the formula with the two products subtracted in the wrong order
computes it with no notion that it measures area scaling
treats a negative determinant as an arithmetic error rather than a flip in orientation

nodes.label: Column space and rank
nodes.blurb: Identifies the span of the columns as the output space and rank as its dimension.
misconceptions: counts rank as the number of columns rather than the number of independent ones
places the column space in the domain rather than the codomain
believes rank can exceed the smaller of the two dimensions

nodes.label: Determinants in general
nodes.blurb: Computes larger determinants and reads zero as the transformation flattening space.
misconceptions: treats it as a formula to grind, with no notion of signed volume scaling
reads det = 0 as the matrix being empty or zero rather than collapsing a dimension
drops the alternating signs during cofactor expansion

nodes.label: Invertibility
nodes.blurb: Knows when a transformation can be undone, and ties that to rank, determinant, and null space.
misconceptions: thinks the inverse is found by taking reciprocals of the entries
believes every square matrix has an inverse
recites that det = 0 means singular but cannot say why collapsing space makes undoing impossible

nodes.label: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues
nodes.blurb: Finds the directions a transformation leaves on their own span, and what it scales them by.
misconceptions: thinks an eigenvector is left completely unchanged rather than kept on its own line
treats the eigenvector as a single vector instead of an entire line of solutions
solves the characteristic polynomial but cannot say what the eigenvalue measures

nodes.label: Change of basis
nodes.blurb: Translates a vector's coordinates between bases and knows which direction the matrix carries you.
misconceptions: applies the change-of-basis matrix in the wrong direction
thinks the vector itself changes rather than its coordinate readout
builds the matrix from the new basis vectors written in the new basis, which is always the identity

nodes.label: Similar matrices
nodes.blurb: Reads P inverse A P as the same transformation described from a different basis.
misconceptions: thinks similar matrices are ones that merely look alike
cannot read the sandwich as 'translate, act, translate back'
expects similar matrices to share visible entries

nodes.label: Diagonalization
nodes.blurb: Chooses an eigenbasis in which the transformation is nothing but scaling along axes.
misconceptions: assumes every matrix is diagonalizable
orders the eigenvalues in D without matching the eigenvector order in P
sees it as a computational trick rather than as choosing the basis where the map is just scaling
